notes.pump: Absorption peaks near 490 nm, so green lasers (532 nm) or direct blue/green diodes work. The ~3 µs upper-state lifetime makes flashlamps impractical.
notes.level: Vibronic 4-level: fast phonon relaxation empties the lower level, giving a very broad gain band.
notes.pumpWavelength: The absorption band spans ~400–600 nm; 532 nm from frequency-doubled Nd or Yb lasers is the classic pump.
notes.lasing: Gain spans ~650–1100 nm, among the broadest of any solid-state gain medium.
notes.transition: Ti³⁺ has a single 3d electron. ²E is the upper state; the lower ²T₂ is vibrationally broadened.
notes.modes: The huge bandwidth supports sub-10 fs pulses through Kerr-lens mode locking.
notes.power: Oscillators are pump-limited; chirped-pulse amplifiers reach mJ–J pulses (TW–PW peak power).
notes.apps: Ultrashort pulses plus tunability drive spectroscopy, microscopy, combs and high-field physics.
notes.lifetime: ~3.2 µs upper-state lifetime — short enough that a flashlamp pulse can't build inversion faster than the state decays, which is exactly why Ti:Sapph needs a CW or pulsed-laser pump instead.

notes.pumpWavelength: Nd:YAG absorbs strongly near 808 nm; 885 nm gives a lower quantum defect.
notes.lasing: 1064 nm is the strongest line, with weaker lines at 946 and 1319 nm.
notes.transition: The upper ⁴F₃/₂ level lives ~230 µs, ideal for energy storage.

notes.power: Scales from watts to kW; Q-switching gives ~10 ns pulses of mJ–J.
notes.apps: Robust and versatile: industry, medicine, ranging, and pumping via frequency doubling.
notes.lifetime: ~230 µs upper-state (⁴F₃/₂) lifetime. Long enough to store pump energy between flashlamp/diode pulses, which is what makes Q-switching to ns, mJ–J pulses straightforward.

notes.pump: Its narrow absorption line near 940 nm wastes most lamp light, so diode pumping is used in practice.
notes.level: Only two manifolds. The lower level sits in ²F₇/₂ and is thermally populated at room temperature, so it is quasi-3-level.
notes.pumpWavelength: 940 nm is broad and easy; the 969 nm zero-phonon line lowers the heat load.
notes.lasing: 1030 nm has a tiny quantum defect (~9%), so heating is low.
notes.transition: Yb³⁺ has just two manifolds: ²F₅/₂ → ²F₇/₂.
notes.modes: The ~9 nm bandwidth supports a few hundred fs, not sub-10 fs.
notes.power: Low heat load enables thin-disk lasers with multi-kW output.
notes.apps: High average power plus fs–ps capability make it the industrial ultrafast workhorse.
notes.lifetime: ~950 µs–1 ms upper-state lifetime — roughly 4× longer than Nd:YAG's. That extra storage capacity is a big part of why Yb:YAG scales so well in high-energy Q-switched and amplified systems.

notes.pump: A DC discharge excites He, which transfers energy to Ne by resonant collisions.
notes.level: The lower neon level (2p₄) empties quickly: a 4-level scheme.
notes.lasing: 632.8 nm dominates; other lines need different mirrors.
notes.transition: Both lasing states are excited neon levels (Paschen notation 3s₂ and 2p₄).
notes.modes: Low gain and little stored energy: HeNe lasers run CW with a very narrow linewidth.
notes.power: Low gain limits output to a few mW, but beam quality and coherence are excellent.
notes.apps: Superb coherence and beam quality suit alignment, metrology and interferometry.

notes.pumpWavelength: Broad absorption in the yellow-green and red covers lamp output and red diodes.
notes.lasing: Tunable ~700–820 nm; 755 nm is the medical standard.
notes.transition: The vibronic ⁴T₂ band lases down to the ⁴A₂ ground state.
notes.modes: The upper-state lifetime (~260 µs) suits long pulses and Q-switching.

notes.apps: 755 nm light is absorbed by melanin, hence hair and pigment treatments.

notes.pump: Two broad absorption bands (~405 nm and ~530–550 nm) overlap well with a xenon flashlamp's output; ruby is essentially always flashlamp-pumped.
notes.level: Ruby is the textbook pure 3-level laser: the lower laser level IS the ground state, so more than half the Cr³⁺ ions must be excited before any gain exists at all — unlike every quasi-3-level or 4-level laser elsewhere in this quiz.
notes.pumpWavelength: The two absorption bands sit in the blue and green-yellow, which is why ruby looks pink/red (it absorbs the complementary colors).
notes.lasing: 694.3 nm (R1) has higher gain and dominates; the weaker R2 line at 692.9 nm is rarely used.
notes.transition: Both the upper (²E) and lower (⁴A₂, ground state) levels are Cr³⁺ states in the sapphire crystal field — the same ion pair that gives alexandrite its R-line, but here it's the *only* lasing transition, not a side effect.
notes.modes: The long (~ms) upper-state lifetime lets ruby store energy for a flashlamp pulse, and early Q-switched ruby lasers were historically important, but the huge pump threshold of a 3-level system rules out practical CW operation.
notes.power: Modern ruby systems are mostly small (~1 J at low rep rate); historic large-aperture ruby amplifier chains reached much higher energies.
notes.apps: Ruby lasers have been largely displaced by better media, but its narrow, highly coherent pulsed red output is still used for holography and pulsed diagnostics.
notes.lifetime: ~3 ms metastable ²E lifetime — long for a solid-state laser, and part of why a single flashlamp pulse can invert enough population, but the true 3-level structure still demands very high pump energy.

notes.pump: A xenon flashlamp's output overlaps Er:YAG's absorption bands around 500, 650 and 750–800 nm; diode or Ti:sapphire pumping near 790 nm is also used.
notes.pumpWavelength: The absorption bands are broad enough to tolerate either flashlamp or diode/Ti:sapphire pumping without precise wavelength matching.
notes.lasing: 2940 nm falls right in a strong water-absorption peak, which is exactly why it's so effective for tissue ablation.
notes.transition: Both levels belong to the ⁴I manifold family of Er³⁺, one level closer to the ground state than the ⁴I9/2 or ⁴S3/2 levels the flashlamp directly excites.
notes.modes: Continuous-wave operation is possible but requires high Er³⁺ doping so that ion-ion cross-relaxation keeps recycling the lower level fast enough.
notes.power: Energy per pulse is modest compared to Nd:YAG because of the self-terminating bottleneck; scaling further usually means higher doping and cross-relaxation, not just more pump power.
notes.apps: 2940 nm is the strongest water absorption band of any common laser line, which drives essentially all of its medical uses.
notes.lifetime: In heavily-doped crystals the upper level (⁴I₁₁/₂) lifetime is ~0.23 ms. See the question above for why the number alone doesn't tell the full story here.

extraQuestions.title: Self-terminating transition
extraQuestions.q: The 2940 nm transition doesn't fit neatly into the usual 3-level/4-level picture. Which of the following are true about it? Select all that apply.

options.t: The lower laser level (⁴I₁₃/₂) actually lives longer than the upper level (⁴I₁₁/₂), so population piles up there and quenches the gain — the transition is self-terminating
Ion–ion cross-relaxation / up-conversion between neighboring Er³⁺ ions is what recycles the lower level fast enough to sustain CW or high-rep-rate output
The lower laser level is the ground state, making this a pure 3-level system like ruby
The upper level empties faster than the lower level, exactly like a textbook 4-level laser
Reaching population inversion requires cryogenic cooling of the crystal

extraQuestions.note: Structurally, both laser levels sit above the ground state (⁴I₁₅/₂), so a simple diagram would label this "4-level." But that label assumes the lower level always empties fast — here it's the opposite: the lower level (⁴I₁₃/₂) outlives the upper one (⁴I₁₁/₂), so every emitted photon leaves behind an ion that blocks further gain until something removes it. High Er³⁺ doping makes ion-ion cross-relaxation and up-conversion fast enough to clear the bottleneck, which is why real Er:YAG lasers work at all — CW operation in particular depends on it.

modes.t: Direct sub-10 fs pulses from the oscillator

power.ok: Tens of W CW (rod/fiber); Q-switched pulses of mJ-level energy
no: Only nJ pulses at GHz rates

notes.pump: The ~785 nm absorption band (³H₆→³H₄) is reachable with the same AlGaAs diode technology used to pump Nd- and Ti:sapph-class lasers, or with a Ti:Sapphire laser in research setups.
notes.level: The terminal level (³F₄) sits close enough to the ground manifold (³H₆) to be thermally populated at room temperature, making this a quasi-3-level transition, the same category as Yb:YAG.
notes.pumpWavelength: 785–786 nm is host-dependent but close enough across Tm-doped crystals that the same diode designs are widely reused.
notes.lasing: The ~2 µm band is strongly absorbed by water and is considered eye-safe at typical operating energies, unlike 1064 nm or 1550 nm.
notes.transition: Both levels are excited-state manifolds of Tm³⁺; ³H₆ is also the ground manifold, which is why the lower level is thermally populated.
notes.modes: The very long upper-state lifetime supports efficient Q-switched energy storage even at modest diode pump power.
notes.power: Efficient cross-relaxation keeps thermal loading low relative to the stored energy, which is part of why Tm systems scale well in fiber and thin-rod geometries.
notes.apps: Eye-safety at 2 µm makes it attractive for LIDAR and outdoor ranging; strong water absorption suits soft-tissue surgery similarly to Er:YAG, just at a different wavelength and with fiber delivery more common.
notes.lifetime: ~15 ms radiative lifetime of the upper level in YAG — about 15× longer than Yb:YAG's. Combined with the two-for-one cross-relaxation process (one absorbed 785 nm pump photon excites two Tm³⁺ ions to the upper laser level), this gives a very low pump-power threshold for a given stored energy, and only a ~20% quantum defect despite the large wavelength gap between pump and laser photons.

extraQuestions.title: Two-for-one cross-relaxation
extraQuestions.q: Tm:YAG's pump-to-laser conversion is often called “two-for-one” cross-relaxation. Which of the following are true about it? Select all that apply.

options.t: One absorbed ~785 nm pump photon can excite two neighboring Tm³⁺ ions to the upper laser level, giving a quantum efficiency approaching 200%
Despite the large energy gap between the ~785 nm pump photon and the ~2010 nm laser photon, the quantum defect is only ~20% because two laser photons emerge per pump photon
It happens inside a single Tm³⁺ ion, with no energy transfer to neighboring ions
It only becomes significant at very low (well under 1%) Tm³⁺ doping concentrations
It increases thermal loading in the crystal compared to an equivalent Yb:YAG laser

extraQuestions.note: The pump excites a Tm³⁺ ion to ³H₄; that ion can then relax to the upper laser level ³F₄ while handing its leftover energy to a neighboring ground-state (³H₆) ion, promoting it to ³F₄ as well — one photon in, two excited ions out. This cross-relaxation is a near-resonant, ion-to-ion energy-transfer process, so it needs Tm³⁺ ions close enough together to interact, which is why it only becomes efficient at higher doping (a few percent Tm³⁺), not lower. The quantum-defect saving is what keeps Tm:YAG's thermal load low relative to its very large pump/laser wavelength gap, and part of why it scales well in fiber and thin-rod geometries.

lasers.name: Diode
lasers.gain: a direct-bandgap III-V semiconductor (e.g. GaAs/AlGaAs, as used in 808 nm pump-diode modules)

lasing.ok: ~808 nm (a common high-power pump-diode line; diode lasers overall span roughly 630–1600+ nm depending on composition)

lasers.transition: Direct band-to-band recombination across the semiconductor bandgap

modes.t: Directly modulated at GHz rates via the drive current
Q-switched via long-term energy storage in the gain medium

power.ok: mW (pointers, telecom) to tens of W per emitter; kW-class from diode bars/stacks
no: Only J-level pulses at low repetition rate

ok: Pump sources for other solid-state lasers (e.g. 808/940 nm modules)

notes.pump: Electrons and holes are injected directly across a forward-biased p–n (or heterostructure) junction — there is no separate optical or discharge pump step at all.
notes.level: Semiconductor gain doesn't come from discrete atomic energy levels: population inversion forms between the conduction and valence bands (or their quasi-Fermi levels) across the direct bandgap, so the atomic-style 3-level/4-level picture used for every other laser in this quiz simply doesn't apply.
notes.pumpWavelength: Not applicable: the excitation is electrical current, not light of any particular wavelength.
notes.lasing: The emission wavelength is set by the semiconductor's bandgap and alloy composition, not by a fixed atomic transition — 808 nm (GaAs/AlGaAs) is singled out here because it's the pump wavelength used throughout the rest of this quiz.
notes.transition: Gain comes from stimulated recombination of electrons and holes across the bandgap, not a transition between two discrete atomic energy levels like every other laser in this set.
notes.modes: The ns-scale carrier lifetime is too short to store meaningful energy for Q-switching, but it's exactly what allows the output to be turned on and off (modulated) at gigahertz rates by modulating the drive current.
notes.power: A single small emitter tops out around tens of W; today's highest-power diode systems stack many emitters into bars and arrays to reach kW-class output for pumping and industrial use.
notes.apps: Nearly every other laser in this quiz that's diode-pumped is ultimately powered by exactly this kind of device.
notes.lifetime: Carrier (spontaneous-emission) lifetime is typically ~1–3 ns — by far the shortest of any laser in this quiz. It rules out Q-switching or the µs–ms energy storage used by ion-doped crystals, but it's exactly why diode lasers can be modulated directly at GHz rates by modulating the drive current — the basis of fiber-optic data transmission.

lasers.name: Excimer (ArF/KrF)
lasers.gain: an argon–fluorine or krypton–fluorine gas mixture forming excited-state dimer molecules (ArF*, KrF*)

lasing.ok: Deep UV: 193 nm (ArF) or 248 nm (KrF), depending on the gas mixture

lasers.transition: ArF*/KrF*: bound excited-dimer (exciplex) state → dissociative (unbound) ground state

modes.t: High repetition rates (up to several kHz) in industrial systems

power.ok: Pulse energies of tens of mJ to ~1 J; average power up to hundreds of W in industrial lithography/micromachining systems
no: Only nJ pulses at GHz rates

notes.pump: A fast, high-voltage electrical discharge (sometimes assisted by electron-beam pre-ionization) excites the Ar/Kr–F₂ gas mixture; the excited-state ArF*/KrF* molecules form only transiently inside the discharge.
notes.level: The lower 'laser level' is a repulsive, unbound molecular state that dissociates within about a picosecond, so it can never accumulate population — making excimer lasers one of the closest real-world approximations to an ideal 4-level system.
notes.lasing: 193 nm (ArF) and 248 nm (KrF) are the two most common excimer lines; other halogen/noble-gas pairs (e.g. XeCl at 308 nm) give other UV wavelengths.
notes.transition: The bound excited dimer relaxes by emitting a UV photon and falling apart into separate, unbound ground-state atoms — the reverse of how the molecule was formed.
notes.modes: The short-lived excited species and the need to continuously re-form fresh molecules rule out CW operation; excimer lasers run in ns pulses set by the discharge duration.
notes.power: High-repetition-rate industrial systems (for lithography and micromachining) trade single-pulse energy for average power, running at hundreds to thousands of Hz.
notes.apps: Deep-UV output enables features and cuts smaller than visible or near-IR lasers can achieve, and 193 nm is strongly absorbed in the outermost layers of the cornea, giving very precise ablation in refractive eye surgery.
notes.lifetime: The bound excited-dimer state has a radiative lifetime of roughly 7-10 ns (measured at 6.8 ns for KrF specifically) — one reason the discharge must keep re-exciting fresh molecules pulse after pulse rather than storing energy the way a long-lived solid-state upper level does.

extraQuestions.title: A ground state that isn't really there
extraQuestions.q: Excimer lasers are unusual among the lasers in this quiz because of what happens to the lower laser level. Which of the following are true? Select all that apply.

options.t: The lower level is a repulsive (unbound) molecular state that falls apart within about a picosecond, so population can never build up there
Because the ground state is unbound, fresh ArF or KrF molecules must be chemically re-formed from Ar/Kr and a fluorine donor (e.g. F₂) inside the discharge on every pulse
Like Nd:YAG's long-lived upper state, the excited-dimer state stores energy efficiently, which is why excimer lasers are usually Q-switched rather than pulsed by the pump itself
The lower level in an excimer laser is a long-lived, bound state — just like the ground state of a HeNe or Nd:YAG laser
Excimer lasers can run continuous-wave in the same way argon-ion or CO₂ lasers do, since the discharge keeps the gain medium continuously excited

extraQuestions.note: Excimer/exciplex molecules (ArF*, KrF*, XeCl*, etc.) only exist as bound species in their electronically excited state — the ground-state potential curve is purely repulsive, so as soon as a molecule emits a photon it flies apart into separate atoms. That means there is structurally no way for the lower laser level to accumulate population, which is exactly the condition a 4-level laser needs, just taken to its logical extreme. But it also means the gain medium has to be rebuilt from scratch every pulse (via fast electrical discharge, reacting Ar/Kr with F₂), and the short (~ns) lifetime of the excited state rules out both Q-switched energy storage and CW operation — unlike Nd:YAG or the CW gas lasers (HeNe, argon-ion, CO₂) elsewhere in this quiz.

lasers.name: Argon-ion (Ar⁺)
lasers.gain: singly-ionized argon gas (Ar⁺) in a high-current arc discharge

lasing.ok: Blue–green, mainly 488.0 and 514.5 nm (several weaker lines between ~450 and 530 nm)

modes.t: Mode-locked ps pulses (used in some research systems)

power.ok: CW output from tens of mW up to a few W; large multi-line 'big-frame' systems reach ~10–20 W, at very low (~0.1%) wall-plug efficiency
no: Only nJ pulses at GHz rates

notes.pump: A high-current DC arc discharge ionizes the argon gas and then excites the resulting Ar⁺ ions by further electron collisions — a two-step process that needs far more electrical power than a neutral-gas discharge like HeNe.
notes.level: The upper laser level is reached by multi-step electron-impact excitation from the Ar⁺ ion ground state; the lower laser level empties quickly via a strongly allowed UV transition (~72–74 nm) back to the ion ground state, giving a classic 4-level scheme.
notes.lasing: 488 nm and 514.5 nm are the two strongest of roughly a dozen visible Ar⁺ lines; intracavity prisms or etalons can select a single line.
notes.transition: Both levels are excited states of the argon ion (not the neutral atom), reached only after the discharge has already stripped an electron from Ar.
notes.modes: The continuously-refreshed high-current discharge sustains a stable CW population inversion; mode-locking is possible but the short upper-state lifetime rules out Q-switching.
notes.power: Ionizing and exciting argon twice over (once to strip the electron, again to reach the upper laser level) makes argon-ion one of the least efficient common lasers, requiring substantial water cooling for anything beyond a few watts.
notes.apps: Strong, stable visible output historically made argon-ion the workhorse pump for dye and Ti:Sapph lasers, and it remains common in microscopy, cytometry and ophthalmology, though diode-pumped solid-state lasers have replaced it in many roles.
notes.lifetime: The upper 4p level's radiative lifetime is only a few to ~10 ns, typical of a strongly allowed atomic transition — far too short to store pump energy, which is why the discharge must continuously re-excite the ions to sustain CW output rather than relying on any energy storage.

lasing.ok: ~1530–1565 nm (telecom C-band; L-band Er-doped fiber extends further)

modes.t: Mode-locked fs–ps pulses (e.g. for frequency combs)

power.ok: mW-level signals in telecom EDFAs; dedicated fiber oscillators/amplifiers commonly reach 1–100 W CW
no: Multi-kW continuous, like an industrial CO₂ laser
Only J-level pulses at low repetition rate

ok: Fiber lasers for materials marking and processing
Dermatology and some surgical uses near 1.5 µm

notes.pump: 980 nm or 1480 nm laser diodes are coupled into the fiber core (or cladding, for high-power designs) via fiber-optic couplers — no free-space optics are needed.
notes.level: The lower laser level (⁴I₁₅/₂) is the ion's ground-state manifold and is thermally populated at room temperature, so — like Yb:YAG and Thulium — this is a quasi-3-level system, not a clean 4-level one.
notes.pumpWavelength: 980 nm ('indirect' pumping, via the fast-decaying ⁴I₁₁/₂ level) avoids exciting ions that would reabsorb the signal, giving the best noise figure — the usual choice for low-noise preamps. 1480 nm ('in-band' pumping, straight into the lower Stark sublevels of ⁴I₁₃/₂) has a smaller quantum defect relative to the ~1550 nm signal, so more of the pump energy becomes signal photons rather than heat — better power-conversion efficiency, the usual choice for high-power booster stages.
notes.lasing: The ⁴I₁₃/₂ → ⁴I₁₅/₂ manifold-to-manifold transition is inhomogeneously broadened by the glass host, giving the broad gain bandwidth that makes silica fiber the backbone of WDM telecom amplification.
notes.transition: Same ion (Er³⁺) as Er:YAG, but a different transition and host: fiber lasing uses ⁴I₁₃/₂ → ⁴I₁₅/₂ near 1.5 µm, not Er:YAG's ⁴I₁₁/₂ → ⁴I₁₃/₂ at 2940 nm.
notes.modes: Fiber's long interaction length and excellent heat dissipation support both efficient CW operation and, with dispersion/nonlinearity management, stable mode-locking for compact fs–ps sources.
notes.power: A single-mode telecom EDFA only needs to amplify mW-level signals, while dedicated high-power Er (or Er/Yb co-doped) fiber lasers scale into the tens-to-hundreds-of-watt range.
notes.apps: The C-band gain window lines up with the telecom fiber's lowest-loss transmission window, which is why EDFAs became the enabling technology for long-haul fiber-optic communication.
notes.lifetime: The ⁴I₁₃/₂ upper level has an unusually long ~10 ms lifetime in silica glass — one of the longest of any common gain medium — letting a fiber amplifier store substantial energy relative to its tiny (µm-scale) mode volume and sustain gain efficiently even at modest pump power.
